## In one sentence

Ecology studies the distribution and abundance of organisms, and the
interactions that produce those patterns across space and time.

## The central idea

Ecological questions are about scale. An organism has traits; a population is a
reproducing group of one species; a community contains interacting species; an
ecosystem includes those organisms plus physical and chemical processes.

A useful workflow is:

1. Define the focal entity and boundary.
2. Choose the spatial and temporal scale.
3. Identify the processes that could cause the pattern.
4. Measure the pattern and compare it with a prediction.

## Niche and habitat

A habitat is where an organism lives. Its niche is the set of environmental
conditions and resources under which it can survive and reproduce, including its
interactions with other organisms. The fundamental niche describes potential
conditions; the realised niche is narrowed by competition, predation, disease,
and dispersal limits.

::: {.callout-important}
A correlation between an organism and an environment does not by itself show
that the environment causes the pattern. Manipulation, natural experiments, or
stronger designs are needed to separate competing explanations.
:::

## Feedback and scale

Negative feedback tends to stabilise a system: crowding can reduce survival or
birth rates. Positive feedback amplifies change: vegetation loss can increase
runoff and erosion, making further vegetation loss more likely. The same system
can be stable at one scale and variable at another.

## Check your understanding

Choose a species near you. Define its habitat, propose its realised niche, and
name one interaction that could prevent it from occupying every suitable site.
